content: Postpartum contraception is essential for improving maternal and child health by increasing the interval between births. For lactating women, the choice of contraception is influenced by concerns about the potential effects of hormones on breast milk quality and quantity, as well as the transfer of hormones to the infant. Ideally, the chosen contraceptive method should not interfere with lactation or the infant's growth. The timing of contraceptive initiation is also critical. While most women have access to healthcare professionals immediately after delivery, many do not return for follow-up contraceptive counseling. However, initiating hormonal contraceptives immediately postpartum may disrupt the establishment of milk production. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of hormonal contraceptives on lactation and infant growth. A comprehensive search for eligible trials was conducted up to March 2, 2015, using multiple databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, POPLINE, Web of Science, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP. Review articles were also examined, and investigators were contacted. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials in any language that compared hormonal contraception with another hormonal method, nonhormonal contraception, or placebo during lactation. Hormonal methods included combined oral contraceptives (COCs), progestin-only pills (POPs), injectable contraceptives, implants, and intrauterine devices (IUDs). Primary outcomes included breast milk quantity or composition, lactation initiation, maintenance or duration, infant growth, and the timing of contraceptive initiation and its effect on lactation. Secondary outcomes included contraceptive efficacy during breastfeeding and birth interval. For continuous variables, the mean difference (MD) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) was calculated. For dichotomous outcomes, the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio (OR) with a 95% CI was used. Due to variations in interventions and outcome measures, the data were not pooled into a meta-analysis. In 2014, seven additional trials were included, bringing the total to 11 trials involving 1,482 women. Four trials evaluated COCs, three studied a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS), two examined POPs, and two assessed the etonogestrel-releasing implant. Many older studies lacked quantified results. Most trials did not report significant differences between study groups in terms of breastfeeding duration, breast milk composition, or infant growth. However, exceptions were noted, primarily in older studies with limited data. Regarding breastfeeding duration, two out of eight trials suggested a negative effect on lactation. One COC study reported a negative impact on lactation duration compared to placebo but did not provide quantified results. Another trial found a lower percentage of women in the LNG-IUS group breastfeeding at 75 days postpartum compared to the nonhormonal IUD group (P < 0.05), but no significant difference was observed at one year. For breast milk volume, two older studies indicated a reduction in milk volume in the COC group compared to placebo. One trial did not quantify the results, while the other reported lower mean milk volumes in the COC group, such as at 16 weeks (MD -24.00 mL, 95% CI -34.53 to -13.47) and at 24 weeks (MD -24.90 mL, 95% CI -36.01 to -13.79). Four other trials, including those evaluating POPs, a COC, or the etonogestrel implant, did not report significant differences in milk volume or composition between groups. Seven trials assessed infant growth. One trial found greater weight gain in the etonogestrel implant group compared to no contraceptive method at six weeks postpartum (MD 426.00 g, 95% CI 58.94 to 793.06), but less weight gain compared to depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) from six to 12 weeks postpartum (MD -271.00 g, 95% CI -355.10 to -186.90). Other trials, which studied POPs, COCs versus POPs, or an LNG-IUS, did not report significant differences in infant growth. The authors concluded that the results across the 11 trials were inconsistent, and the evidence for any specific hormonal contraceptive method was limited. The overall quality of evidence was moderate, but three out of four placebo-controlled trials of COCs or POPs were rated as low quality. A sensitivity analysis of six trials with moderate-quality evidence and sufficient outcome data found no significant differences between groups in breastfeeding duration for etonogestrel implant insertion times, COC versus POP, or LNG-IUS. For breast milk volume or composition, one COC study showed a negative effect, while an implant trial reported no significant difference. Of the four trials assessing infant growth, three found no significant differences between groups. One trial reported greater weight gain in the etonogestrel implant group compared to no method, but less weight gain compared to DMPA.
